imperialism

/im-PEER-ee-uh-liz-uhm/ - the stress falls on PEER · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Imperialism means a nation's policy of extending its power over other lands and peoples and running them for its own gain.

The atlas of 1900 wears imperialism on its face: half of Africa printed in the colors of four European capitals.

Example

The kingdom of Veyra never planted a single overseas colony, yet by 1890 its imperialism ran along two thousand miles of foreign coastline. Client princes kept their thrones so long as Veyran advisers approved their budgets; Veyran mints printed the coastal states' coinage; and when one sultan objected, a gunboat anchored offshore until he stopped objecting.

Veyra shows why imperialism is the bigger word: it names the whole policy of commanding other lands and peoples for the home country's gain, whatever the instrument — conquest, colonies, debt, advisers, or a gunboat riding at anchor. Settling foreign soil is one tool of that policy, but as Veyra proves, the policy never required it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

colonization: Colonization is one instrument of empire: the planting of settlers on foreign soil to hold and work it for the home country. Imperialism is the whole policy — conquest, colonies, debt, and gunboats all serve it, and it can run an 'independent' country without settling a single family there.

expansionism: Expansionism names the appetite — the drive to enlarge a nation's territory, markets, or reach. Imperialism is the appetite grown into a system: not just wanting more, but ruling what is swallowed and running it from the center.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

isolationism: a policy of staying out of other nations' affairs

independence: a people governing itself, free of outside command

Where it sits · how completely other peoples are brought under command

expansionism → imperialism → subjugation

expansionism vs. imperialism: Expansionism is milder than imperialism: it names the appetite for more territory or markets, while imperialism is the full policy of ruling other lands and peoples once they are reached.

subjugation vs. imperialism: Subjugation goes further than imperialism: an imperial power may rule through governors, clients, and commerce, but subjugation crushes a people's own institutions until nothing answers back.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — imper: to command (Latin imperare)

Suffix — -ial: relating to

Suffix — -ism: a policy, doctrine, or practice

Put it together: Imperare, 'to command,' built imperium — Rome's word for supreme command itself — and imperium built empire. Add -ism, the suffix English hangs on a doctrine, and imperialism is literally 'command as policy': the practice of a nation commanding lands beyond its own.

Use the root in a new word: imperious: Critics found the conductor imperious in rehearsal and unfailingly gracious at dinner.

Word Choice

critical / historical-political

Imperialism is a charge as much as a description: a nation extending command over other lands and running them for its own gain. Colonization, taught beside it in this unit, is one instrument of that policy — settlers planted to stay. And when the dominance works by deference instead of command — no veto, no garrison, others simply follow — this unit's hegemony is the sharper word.
